subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Battery Recycling
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Battery Recycling.

hook.text: Millions of EV batteries will reach end of life in the next decade—what happens to all that metal?

buildup.text: Recycling recovers lithium, nickel, cobalt, and other valuable metals from spent battery cells.

discovery.text: Hydrometallurgical processes dissolve the cathode in acid and extract each metal for reuse in new cells.

twist.text: Recycled metals can be just as pure as freshly mined ones, creating a true circular supply chain.

climax.text: Redwood Materials and Li-Cycle are building massive recycling plants to handle the coming wave of retired packs.

punchline.text: Tomorrow's batteries will be made from yesterday's batteries.

quiz.question: What can battery recycling recover from spent EV cells?
options: Lithium, nickel, cobalt, and other metals

details.summary: EV battery recycling recovers valuable materials like lithium, cobalt, and nickel from spent packs through hydrometallurgical or pyrometallurgical processes, reducing waste and mining dependence.
details.whyItMatters: Millions of EV batteries will reach end-of-life in the coming decade. Effective recycling is essential to keep rare materials in circulation and prevent a mountain of hazardous electronic waste.
takeaways: Recycling recovers lithium, cobalt, nickel, and copper
Hydrometallurgy uses chemical baths to dissolve and separate metals
Recycling reduces the need for new mining of critical minerals

faq.question: Can all the materials in an EV battery be recycled?
faq.answer: Current processes recover over 95 percent of nickel, cobalt, and copper. Lithium recovery rates are improving rapidly but were historically lower. New direct recycling methods aim to recover nearly everything.

faq.question: Is EV battery recycling currently profitable?
faq.answer: Profitability depends on the metals recovered. Batteries rich in cobalt and nickel are more valuable to recycle. As battery chemistries shift to cheaper materials, recycling economics may require policy support.
